We need to interpret the problem: It says "beauty" and "minimum possible beauty" but also defines "ugliness" as the length of longest subsequence consisting of unequal elements.

Actually, they want minimal ugliness after operations: we can replace each element with any integer in [nums[i] - k, nums[i] + k] (but each index at most once). After operations, we want to minimize the length of longest subsequence consisting of unequal elements.

But note: In the examples, output for Example 1: after operations array [4,4,1,4]; they say ugliness is 1 (only one pair of unequal elements). Wait, they define ugliness as length of longest subsequence consisting of unequal elements. In array [4,4,1,4], longest subsequence with all unequal elements? Let's consider: you can pick at most one element of each value? Actually subsequence of unequal elements: the subsequence must contain pairwise unequal elements (i.e., all elements are distinct). Longest such subsequence is the number of distinct values present? Because you can pick each distinct value at most once while preserving order. So the length of longest subsequence with all elements distinct equals number of distinct values present? Not exactly: if you have duplicate values you could still take one of them; you cannot take two equal elements because then they'd be equal. So the maximum length of a subsequence with all elements distinct is the number of distinct values in the array. Indeed you can select one occurrence of each distinct value, picking them in order of appearance yields a subsequence of distinct elements. So ugliness = number of distinct values in the array after operations. Example: [4,4,1,4] has distinct values {1,4} -> 2 distinct. But they claim ugliness is 1? Wait they said "only one pair of unequal elements". Perhaps they define ugliness differently: maybe as count of pairs (i, j) with i<j and nums[i] != nums[j]?
